reference.source: Soft tissue and vascular tumour pathology references
clinicalPearls: Vascular tumour of endothelial origin occupying an intermediate grade between benign haemangioma and high-grade angiosarcoma.
The WWTR1 (TAZ)-CAMTA1 fusion is the molecular hallmark in most cases; a minority carry a YAP1-TFE3 fusion and tend to occur in younger patients.
Frequently multifocal, affecting liver, lung, bone and soft tissue; hepatic disease often mimics metastatic carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma.
Pulmonary disease typically presents as multiple bilateral nodules and may cause cough, pleuritic pain or haemoptysis.
Characteristic histology shows epithelioid endothelial cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles ('blister cells') set in a myxohyaline stroma.
Endothelial markers (CD31, CD34, ERG, FLI-1) are positive; nuclear CAMTA1 staining strongly supports the diagnosis.
The clinical course is unpredictable, ranging from indolent over many years to rapidly progressive.
There is no standard chemotherapy; options span active surveillance, surgery for localised disease, and systemic anti-angiogenic or mTOR-directed therapy for progression.
reference.pathophysiology: Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant vascular neoplasm arising from endothelial cells and occupying an intermediate position on the spectrum between benign haemangioma and high-grade angiosarcoma. The defining molecular event in most cases is a balanced translocation generating the WWTR1 (TAZ)-CAMTA1 fusion oncoprotein, which dysregulates Hippo pathway signalling and drives constitutive transcriptional activity and endothelial proliferation; a distinct minority harbour a YAP1-TFE3 fusion and tend to show more vasoformative morphology in younger patients. Tumour cells are epithelioid with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and characteristic intracytoplasmic lumina (vacuoles) that may contain red cells, set within a myxohyaline or chondroid matrix. Growth is often infiltrative along vascular channels, and apparent multifocality, for example multiple hepatic or pulmonary lesions, frequently reflects multicentric origin rather than distant metastasis.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the affected site (hepatic lesions may show a target or halo appearance)
Immunohistochemistry (CD31, CD34, ERG, FLI-1, CAMTA1, TFE3)
Molecular testing for WWTR1-CAMTA1 or YAP1-TFE3 fusion
FDG-PET/CT for staging and detection of multifocal disease
Dedicated chest imaging for pulmonary involvement
Liver function tests where hepatic disease is present
redFlags: Pleural or peritoneal effusions, which are associated with a worse outcome
Rapid tumour growth or new constitutional symptoms such as weight loss
Multiorgan involvement with declining performance status
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable, with some tumours pursuing an indolent course over years while others progress rapidly. Adverse features include large tumour size, high mitotic activity and the presence of pleural or peritoneal effusions.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as carcinoma or metastasis because of the epithelioid morphology and occasional keratin positivity.
Assuming multifocal disease represents incurable metastatic spread rather than multicentric primary disease.
Overtreating indolent, asymptomatic disease that may be suitable for surveillance.
Omitting confirmatory immunohistochemistry (CAMTA1) or molecular fusion testing.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone references
management: Recognise that clinical course is highly variable and multifocal disease (limb, liver, or lung) does not necessarily represent conventional metastasis; presence of metastatic disease alone should not preclude resection or transplantation
For localised, resectable bone or soft tissue disease, or a solitary hepatic lesion, surgical resection is the treatment of choice and offers the best chance of durable control
For unresectable multifocal hepatic disease, a short period of observation with close monitoring is a reasonable first step to help decide among observation, ablation, resection, or transplantation
Consider liver transplantation for disease confined to the liver but not amenable to resection, even in the presence of distant metastatic disease
Reserve systemic therapy for disease that is progressive or symptomatic rather than using it as routine adjuvant treatment
Systemic options that have been used include chemotherapy, VEGF-pathway inhibitor (antiangiogenic) therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, though evidence is limited by disease rarity
Antiangiogenic therapy is a reasonable systemic option for progressive disease based on phase II data showing disease control (slowed progression or partial response) in most treated patients

Outside a clinical trial, mTOR-pathway inhibition and interferon-based therapy are also used in sarcoma practice, with cytotoxic chemotherapy generally reserved for more aggressive, angiosarcoma-like behaviour (general oncology standard, not from DeVita)

No defined role for radiotherapy is described for this tumour, but palliative radiotherapy can be considered for painful bony lesions not amenable to surgery, as for other bone and soft tissue sarcomas (general oncology standard, not from DeVita)
Patients managed with observation require serial monitoring to detect progression, since treatment decisions in multifocal disease are guided by watching for change over time
Track disease with cross-sectional imaging at an individualised frequency based on disease pace rather than a fixed schedule (general oncology standard, not from DeVita)
Refer to a centre experienced with vascular tumours or sarcoma for management decisions in multifocal or hepatic disease, given the rarity and case-by-case nature of the decision
Refer early for transplant evaluation when hepatic disease is confined to the liver but not resectable
Refer to medical oncology for consideration of systemic therapy once disease is progressing or symptomatic
